column1: What makes a SQL subquery correlated?
column2:
It references a column from an outer query.
The inner query depends on values supplied by the outer query.
Review source

column1: Why can a correlated subquery not run unchanged by itself?
column2:
It needs values supplied by the outer query.
Its outer references are not defined by the inner query alone.
Review source

column1: What can replace separate per-row subquery execution in an optimized correlated-query plan?
column2:
An equivalent join.
Correlation describes logical dependency rather than a required physical execution strategy.
Review source

column1: What can happen when an unqualified subquery column exists only in the outer query?
column2:
SQL Server can bind it to the outer column.
Qualify columns with table aliases to prevent unintended correlation.
Review source

column1: With non-NULL category IDs, which group does a category-correlated AVG calculate for each product?
column2:
The current product's category.
An ordinary category-equality predicate does not exclude the product itself.
Review source

column1: What value does a SELECT-list scalar subquery produce when it returns no rows?
column2:
NULL.
Zero rows are allowed in scalar position rather than requiring exactly one row.
Review source

column1: What happens if a SELECT-list scalar subquery returns more than one row?
column2:
SQL Server raises an error.
Multiple rows cannot supply a single scalar value.
Review source

column1: What does a customer's correlated COUNT(*) return for no orders, without GROUP BY or HAVING?
column2:
0.
It counts an empty matching set rather than returning a missing scalar.
Review source

column1: What does a SELECT-list correlated aggregate add without grouping the outer query?
column2:
A calculated value for each outer row.
It does not collapse those rows into category or customer groups.
Review source

column1: Why does WHERE EXISTS not multiply an outer customer row when several orders match?
column2:
It filters the row rather than joining in every matching order.
The number of matching inner rows does not multiply the outer row.
Review source

column1: What does the 1 mean in EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ...)?
column2:
An arbitrary selected value, not a row limit.
EXISTS tests row presence rather than the chosen value.
Review source

column1: Why does EXISTS(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.Orders WHERE 1 = 0) still find a row?
column2:
An ungrouped COUNT returns one row containing zero.
EXISTS tests the aggregate row rather than whether the count is positive.
Review source

column1: Why does a NOT EXISTS test for price violations also accept an empty category?
column2:
There are no violating rows for NOT EXISTS to find.
Require product existence separately if empty categories must be excluded.
Review source

column1: Why can rejecting Price <= 100 through NOT EXISTS still accept a category with NULL prices?
column2:
The NULL comparison is UNKNOWN and does not select a violating row.
Include Price IS NULL in the violation test if missing prices must fail.
Review source

column1: Why is correlated TOP (3) ORDER BY Price DESC unstable when prices tie?
column2:
Tied rows lack a unique ordering.
Add a unique key to make the chosen membership repeatable.
Review source

column1: Within a category, how does counting strictly higher-priced rows treat equal-price products?
column2:
They have the same count and qualify together.
Top-N filters using this count can return more than N rows.
Review source

column1: A category has prices 100, 100, 90, 80. Which price has at least three higher-priced rows?
column2:
80.
The count includes both 100-priced rows rather than just distinct prices.
Review source

column1: For outer order o, which orders does o2.OrderDate < o.OrderDate exclude when timestamps tie?
column2:
Every order at o's timestamp.
It finds an earlier timestamp rather than a preceding row within that timestamp.
Review source

column1: Why must a previous-order lookup correlate on CustomerID?
column2:
To search only the current customer's order history.
Without that condition, another customer's order can become the candidate.
Review source

column1: What can an index on correlation keys reduce?
column2:
The work needed to find matching inner rows.
The optimizer still decides whether to seek or scan.
Review source

column1: Why consider an index on (CategoryID, Price) for a category-correlated price query?
column2:
It supports category lookups with Price available in the index.
It does not guarantee a single index seek.
Review source

column1: With non-NULL CategoryIDs, how can a grouped join replace a correlated category-average lookup?
column2:
Group by CategoryID, calculate AVG(Price), then join to Product.
Use the same source rows and filters to preserve the calculation.
Review source

column1: What must you compare before claiming EXISTS is faster than IN?
column2:
Execution plans and performance on representative data.
The keyword alone does not establish that one equivalent query is faster.
Review source

column1: What reveals whether SQL Server transformed a correlated subquery into a join?
column2:
The execution plan.
Inspect the chosen operators rather than inferring execution from the query text.
Review source

column1: What do logical reads measure in SET STATISTICS IO output?
column2:
Pages read from the data cache.
Compare this work when evaluating a correlated query and its rewrite.
Review source

column1: Why must correlated-query benchmarks use realistic outer-row counts?
column2:
Repeated inner work can become costly as the outer input grows.
A fast small-data test does not establish production performance.
Review source
